title: Mastering the Scleral Buckle: A Retinal Surgeon’s Guide
summary: The scleral buckle remains a cornerstone of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) repair, utilizing scleral indentation to relieve vitreoretinal traction. This comprehensive overview details the surgical principles, patient selection, and intraoperative management required for successful anatomical reattachment.

sections.title: Definition & Indications
sections.content: Scleral buckling is an extraocular procedure designed to repair RRD by creating an indentation of the scleral wall to close retinal breaks and relieve vitreous traction. Primary indications include: young phakic patients, dialysis-related detachments, breaks in multiple quadrants, and patients with high myopia where vitrectomy may induce accelerated cataract formation.

sections.title: Red Flags: Intraoperative & Post-op
content: Ischemia of the anterior segment (encircling band too tight)
Erosion of element through the conjunctiva
Severe post-op pain (suggesting tight element or high IOP)

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: 360-degree peritomy and isolation of the four rectus muscles using 2-0 silk sutures.
Step 2: Indirect ophthalmoscopy to localize all retinal breaks (cryotherapy applied around margins).
Step 3: Placement of mattress sutures (e.g., 5-0 dacron or nylon) for buckle anchoring.
Step 4: Drainage of subretinal fluid (SRF) if needed (external drainage via sclerotomy).
Step 5: Tightening of the buckle element to ensure the break is centered on the ridge.
Step 6: Closure of conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A well-placed buckle should have a 'fish-mouth' appearance on the ridge.
Avoid encircling band tension if the IOP rises excessively during the tightening phase.
Always perform a thorough 360-degree scleral depression search pre-operatively.
SRF drainage is rarely necessary in modern practice unless the break cannot be closed.

sections.title: Landmark Advances
sections.content: The Scleral Buckling vs. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (SPR) study established that while vitrectomy is superior for PVR, scleral buckling remains statistically equivalent or superior for non-PVR detachments in phakic patients, avoiding the long-term risk of nuclear sclerotic cataract formation associated with vitrectomy.
